<p><b>Mario Draghi</b> (<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1177148991">.mw-parser-output .IPA-label-small{font-size:85%}.mw-parser-output .references .IPA-label-small,.mw-parser-output .infobox .IPA-label-small,.mw-parser-output .navbox .IPA-label-small{font-size:100%}</style><span class="IPA-label IPA-label-small">Italian:</span> <span class="IPA nowrap" lang="it-Latn-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian" title="Help:IPA/Italian">[ˈmaːrjo<span class="wrap"> </span>ˈdraːɡi]</a></span>; born 3 September 1947) is an Italian politician, economist, academic, banker, statesman, and civil servant, who served as the <a href="/wiki/Prime_minister_of_Italy" class="mw-redirect" title="Prime minister of Italy">prime minister of Italy</a> from 13 February 2021 to 22 October 2022.<sup id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Prior to his appointment as prime minister, he served as the <a href="/wiki/President_of_the_European_Central_Bank" title="President of the European Central Bank">president of the European Central Bank</a> (ECB) between 2011 and 2019. Draghi was also the chair of the <a href="/wiki/Financial_Stability_Board" title="Financial Stability Board">Financial Stability Board</a> between 2009 and 2011, and <a href="/wiki/Governor_of_the_Bank_of_Italy" title="Governor of the Bank of Italy">governor of the Bank of Italy</a> between 2006 and 2011.<sup id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-4"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>After working as an economist, Draghi worked for the <a href="/wiki/World_Bank" class="mw-redirect" title="World Bank">World Bank</a> in Washington, D.C., throughout the 1980s, and in 1991 returned to <a href="/wiki/Rome" title="Rome">Rome</a> to become <a href="/wiki/Director_general_of_the_Italian_Treasury" class="mw-redirect" title="Director general of the Italian Treasury">director general of the Italian Treasury</a>. He left that role after a decade to join <a href="/wiki/Goldman_Sachs" title="Goldman Sachs">Goldman Sachs</a>, where he remained until his appointment as governor of the Bank of Italy in 2006. His tenure as Governor coincided with the <a href="/wiki/Great_Recession_in_Europe" title="Great Recession in Europe">2008 Great Recession</a>, and in the midst of this he was selected to become the first chair of the <a href="/wiki/Financial_Stability_Board" title="Financial Stability Board">Financial Stability Board</a>, the global standard-setter that replaced the <a href="/wiki/Financial_Stability_Forum" title="Financial Stability Forum">Financial Stability Forum</a>.
</p><p>He left those roles after his nomination by the <a href="/wiki/European_Council" title="European Council">European Council</a> in 2011 to serve as president of the ECB. He presided over the institution during the <a href="/wiki/Eurozone_crisis" class="mw-redirect" title="Eurozone crisis">Eurozone crisis</a>, becoming famous throughout Europe for saying that he would be prepared to do "whatever it takes" to prevent the <a href="/wiki/Euro" title="Euro">euro</a> from failing.<sup id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-5"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>  In 2014, Draghi was listed by <i><a href="/wiki/Forbes_Magazine%27s_List_of_The_World%27s_Most_Powerful_People" class="mw-redirect" title="Forbes Magazine's List of The World's Most Powerful People">Forbes</a></i> as the eighth-most powerful person in the world. In 2015, <i><a href="/wiki/Fortune_(magazine)" title="Fortune (magazine)">Fortune</a></i> magazine ranked him as the world's "second greatest leader".<sup id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-7"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He is also the only Italian to be listed three times in the <i><a href="/wiki/Time_100" title="Time 100">Time 100</a></i> annual <a href="/wiki/Listicle" title="Listicle">listicle</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-8"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 2019, <a href="/wiki/Paul_Krugman" title="Paul Krugman">Paul Krugman</a> described him as "the greatest <a href="/wiki/Central_bank" title="Central bank">central banker</a> of modern times."<sup id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-9"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Moreover, thanks to his monetary policies, he is widely considered the "saviour of the euro" during the <a href="/wiki/Euro_area_crisis" title="Euro area crisis">Euro area crisis</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-11"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-12"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He has been nicknamed <i><a href="/wiki/Mario" title="Mario">Super Mario</a></i> by some media, a nickname that was popularised during his time as president of the ECB, when he was credited by numerous sources as having played a key role in combatting the <a href="/wiki/Eurozone_crisis" class="mw-redirect" title="Eurozone crisis">Eurozone crisis</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-13"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-14"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>After Draghi's term as ECB President ended in 2019, he initially returned to private life. On 3 February 2021, in the midst of the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Italy" title="COVID-19 pandemic in Italy">COVID-19 pandemic in Italy</a>, Draghi was invited by President <a href="/wiki/Sergio_Mattarella" title="Sergio Mattarella">Sergio Mattarella</a> to form a <a href="/wiki/Government_of_national_unity" class="mw-redirect" title="Government of national unity">government of national unity</a> (<a href="/wiki/Draghi_Cabinet" class="mw-redirect" title="Draghi Cabinet">Draghi Cabinet</a>), following <a href="/wiki/2021_Italian_government_crisis" title="2021 Italian government crisis">the resignation</a> of <a href="/wiki/Giuseppe_Conte" title="Giuseppe Conte">Giuseppe Conte</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After successful negotiations with parties including the <a href="/wiki/Lega_(political_party)" title="Lega (political party)">League</a> (Lega - Salvini Premier), the <a href="/wiki/Five_Star_Movement" title="Five Star Movement">Five Star Movement</a> (M5S), the <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Party_(Italy)" title="Democratic Party (Italy)">Democratic Party</a> (PD), and <span title="Italian-language text"><span lang="it" style="font-style: normal;"><a href="/wiki/Forza_Italia_(2013)" title="Forza Italia (2013)">Forza Italia</a></span></span> (FI), Draghi was sworn in as prime minister on 11 February,<sup id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> pledging to oversee effective implementation of COVID-19 economic stimulus.<sup id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-19"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi was rated highly in public opinion polls in Italy during his time as prime minister; at the end of his first year in office <i><a href="/wiki/Politico_Europe" title="Politico Europe">Politico Europe</a></i> ranked him as the most powerful person in Europe and <i><a href="/wiki/The_Economist" title="The Economist">The Economist</a></i> named Italy as "Country of the Year", singling out Draghi's leadership as central to its nomination.<sup id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-wantedinrome.com_21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wantedinrome.com-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 14 July 2022, the M5S revoked support to Draghi's coalition government regarding a <a href="/wiki/Decree" title="Decree">decree</a> concerning economic stimulus to offset the energy crisis. On the same day, despite having won a <a href="/wiki/Confidence_vote" class="mw-redirect" title="Confidence vote">confidence vote</a>, Draghi announced his resignation as prime minister, which was rejected by President Mattarella.<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 21 July, Draghi resigned for a second time following the failure of a confidence vote to pass with an <a href="/wiki/Absolute_majority" class="mw-redirect" title="Absolute majority">absolute majority</a> due to the withdrawals of M5S, Lega, and FI. On the same day, President Mattarella accepted the resignation and Draghi remained in office as caretaker prime minister.<sup id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He was succeeded by <a href="/wiki/Giorgia_Meloni" title="Giorgia Meloni">Giorgia Meloni</a> on 22 October 2022.<sup id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc">
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Early_life_and_education">Early life and education</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Early life and education"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Mario Draghi was born in <a href="/wiki/Rome" title="Rome">Rome</a> in 1947 to an upper-class family; his father Carlo, who was born in <a href="/wiki/Padua" title="Padua">Padua</a>, Veneto, first joined the <a href="/wiki/Banca_d%27Italia" class="mw-redirect" title="Banca d'Italia">Bank of Italy</a> in 1922, and later worked for the <a href="/wiki/Istituto_per_la_Ricostruzione_Industriale" title="Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale">Institute for Industrial Reconstruction</a> (IRI) and for the <a href="/wiki/Banca_Nazionale_del_Lavoro" title="Banca Nazionale del Lavoro">Banca Nazionale del Lavoro</a>; while his mother, Gilda Mancini, who was born in <a href="/wiki/Monteverde,_Campania" title="Monteverde, Campania">Monteverde, Campania</a>, near <a href="/wiki/Avellino" title="Avellino">Avellino</a>, was a pharmacist. He is the eldest of three children including Andreina, an <a href="/wiki/Art_history" title="Art history">art historian</a>, and Marcello, an entrepreneur.<sup id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> When he was 15 years old, his father died; at 19, his mother died.<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>28<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Draghi studied at the <a href="/wiki/Massimiliano_Massimo_Institute" title="Massimiliano Massimo Institute">Massimiliano Massimo Institute</a>, a <a href="/wiki/Jesuit" class="mw-redirect" title="Jesuit">Jesuit</a> school in Rome, where he was a classmate of the future chairman of <a href="/wiki/Ferrari" title="Ferrari">Ferrari</a>, <a href="/wiki/Luca_Cordero_di_Montezemolo" class="mw-redirect" title="Luca Cordero di Montezemolo">Luca Cordero di Montezemolo</a>, the future prefect and civil servant <a href="/wiki/Giovanni_De_Gennaro_(police_officer)" title="Giovanni De Gennaro (police officer)">Gianni De Gennaro</a> and the future television presenter <a href="/wiki/Giancarlo_Magalli" title="Giancarlo Magalli">Giancarlo Magalli</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 1970, he graduated with honours in economics at the <a href="/wiki/Sapienza_University_of_Rome" title="Sapienza University of Rome">Sapienza University of Rome</a>, under the supervision of Keynesian economist <a href="/wiki/Federico_Caff%C3%A8" title="Federico Caffè">Federico Caffè</a>; his graduation <a href="/wiki/Dissertation" class="mw-redirect" title="Dissertation">dissertation</a> was titled "<a href="/wiki/Economic_integration" title="Economic integration">Economic integration</a> and the variation of <a href="/wiki/Exchange_rate" title="Exchange rate">exchange rates</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In his dissertation, Draghi was particularly critical of Luxembourg Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Pierre_Werner" title="Pierre Werner">Pierre Werner</a>'s remarks that <a href="/wiki/Economic_and_Monetary_Union_of_the_European_Union" title="Economic and Monetary Union of the European Union">European monetary union</a> was "premature".<sup id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi went on to earn a PhD in economics from the <a href="/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology" title="Massachusetts Institute of Technology">Massachusetts Institute of Technology</a> in 1977. His dissertation was titled "Essays on economic theory and applications", completed under the supervision of <a href="/wiki/Franco_Modigliani" title="Franco Modigliani">Franco Modigliani</a> and <a href="/wiki/Robert_Solow" title="Robert Solow">Robert Solow</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Professor_and_civil_servant">Professor and civil servant</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Professor and civil servant"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>From 1975 to 1981, Draghi was first professor of economic and financial policy at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Trento" title="University of Trento">University of Trento</a>, then of <a href="/wiki/Macroeconomics" title="Macroeconomics">macroeconomics</a> at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Padua" title="University of Padua">University of Padua</a>, and later of <a href="/wiki/Mathematical_economics" title="Mathematical economics">mathematical economics</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Ca%27_Foscari_University_of_Venice" title="Ca' Foscari University of Venice">Ca' Foscari University of Venice</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 1981, he was appointed professor of economic and monetary policy at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Florence" title="University of Florence">University of Florence</a> a position that he held until 1994.<sup id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During this time, he also spent time as executive director of the <a href="/wiki/World_Bank" class="mw-redirect" title="World Bank">World Bank</a> in Washington, D.C. In 1983, Draghi was also appointed a counsellor to then-<a href="/wiki/Italian_Minister_of_Treasury" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian Minister of Treasury">Minister of Treasury</a> <a href="/wiki/Giovanni_Goria" title="Giovanni Goria">Giovanni Goria</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In 1991, Minister of Treasury <a href="/wiki/Guido_Carli" title="Guido Carli">Guido Carli</a> and Bank of Italy Governor <a href="/wiki/Carlo_Azeglio_Ciampi" title="Carlo Azeglio Ciampi">Carlo Azeglio Ciampi</a> appointed Draghi as director general of the <a href="/wiki/Ministry_of_Economy_and_Finance_(Italy)#Organization" title="Ministry of Economy and Finance (Italy)">Italian Treasury</a>; Draghi held this senior position in the civil service until 2001.<sup id="cite_ref-GhatakKallianiotis2013_37-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GhatakKallianiotis2013-37"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During his time at the Treasury, he chaired the committee that revised Italian corporate and financial legislation, and drafted the law that continues to govern Italian financial markets.<sup id="cite_ref-PhD2013_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PhD2013-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi was also among the main proponents of the <a href="/wiki/Privatisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Privatisation">privatisations</a> of many state-owned companies which occurred in the Italian economy through the 1990s. He also chaired the management committee of <a href="/wiki/Servizi_Assicurativi_del_Commercio_Estero" class="mw-redirect" title="Servizi Assicurativi del Commercio Estero">SACE</a>, implementing a complete reformation of the group and managing the transition from the <i><a href="/wiki/Mani_Pulite" class="mw-redirect" title="Mani Pulite">Mani Pulite</a></i> corruption scandal. Draghi returned to chair SACE between 1998 and 2001, before the subsequent privatisation. During these years, he was also a board member of several Italian banks and corporations, like <a href="/wiki/Eni" title="Eni">Eni</a>, <a href="/wiki/Istituto_per_la_Ricostruzione_Industriale" title="Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale">Institute for Industrial Reconstruction</a>, <a href="/wiki/Banca_Nazionale_del_Lavoro" title="Banca Nazionale del Lavoro">Banca Nazionale del Lavoro</a> and Istituto Mobiliare Italiano.<sup id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-IRI_40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-IRI-40"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In 2001, he left the Treasury to become a fellow of the Institute of Politics at the <a href="/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_School_of_Government" class="mw-redirect" title="John F. Kennedy School of Government">John F. Kennedy School of Government</a> at <a href="/wiki/Harvard_University" title="Harvard University">Harvard University</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi was also appointed as vice chairman and managing director of <a href="/wiki/Goldman_Sachs" title="Goldman Sachs">Goldman Sachs International</a> in 2002. He was also made a member of the firm's management committee, holding all of these roles until 2005.<sup id="cite_ref-accounting-tricks_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-accounting-tricks-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He led Goldman Sachs's European strategy and its engagements with major European corporations and governments.<sup id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After the revelation that off-market swaps had been systematically used by the <a href="/wiki/Greek_Government" class="mw-redirect" title="Greek Government">Greek Government</a>, facilitated by Goldman Sachs, Draghi stated that he "knew nothing" about the arrangement, and "had nothing to do with it".<sup id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During this period, Draghi also worked as a <a href="/wiki/Trustee" title="Trustee">trustee</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Institute_for_Advanced_Study" title="Institute for Advanced Study">Institute for Advanced Study</a> in <a href="/wiki/Princeton,_New_Jersey" title="Princeton, New Jersey">Princeton, New Jersey</a>, and also spent time as an honorary trustee at the <a href="/wiki/Brookings_Institution" title="Brookings Institution">Brookings Institution</a> in Washington, D.C.<sup id="cite_ref-PhD2013_38-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PhD2013-38"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Governor_of_the_Bank_of_Italy_(2006–2011)"><span id="Governor_of_the_Bank_of_Italy_.282006.E2.80.932011.29"></span>Governor of the Bank of Italy (2006–2011)</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Governor of the Bank of Italy (2006–2011)"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_George_W._Bush_greets_Bank_of_Italy_Governor_and_Financial_Stability_Forum_Chairman_Mario_Draghi.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/President_George_W._Bush_greets_Bank_of_Italy_Governor_and_Financial_Stability_Forum_Chairman_Mario_Draghi.jpg/250px-President_George_W._Bush_greets_Bank_of_Italy_Governor_and_Financial_Stability_Forum_Chairman_Mario_Draghi.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/President_George_W._Bush_greets_Bank_of_Italy_Governor_and_Financial_Stability_Forum_Chairman_Mario_Draghi.jpg/500px-President_George_W._Bush_greets_Bank_of_Italy_Governor_and_Financial_Stability_Forum_Chairman_Mario_Draghi.jpg 2x" data-file-width="514" data-file-height="343"></a><figcaption>Draghi with U.S. President <a href="/wiki/George_W._Bush" title="George W. Bush">George W. Bush</a> in 2008</figcaption></figure>
<p>In December 2005, it was announced that Draghi would become <a href="/wiki/Governor_of_the_Bank_of_Italy" title="Governor of the Bank of Italy">governor of the Bank of Italy</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Prins2009_45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Prins2009-45"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He officially took up the position on 16 January 2006. In April 2006, he was elected by fellow central bank governors to become chairman of the <a href="/wiki/Financial_Stability_Forum" title="Financial Stability Forum">Financial Stability Forum</a>; this body would later be re-organised to become the <a href="/wiki/Financial_Stability_Board" title="Financial Stability Board">Financial Stability Board</a> in April 2009 on behalf of the <a href="/wiki/G20" title="G20">G20</a>, bringing together representatives of governments, central banks and national supervisors institutions in the wake of the <a href="/wiki/Great_Recession" title="Great Recession">financial crisis</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-RadoselovicsMonsálvez2012_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RadoselovicsMonsálvez2012-46"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As the inaugural FSB chairman, Draghi was responsible to the G20 leaders, and worked to promote international financial stability during the <a href="/wiki/Euro_area_crisis" title="Euro area crisis">Euro area crisis</a>, improve the functioning of markets and reduce systemic risk through information exchange and international cooperation between supervisors.
</p><p>In his capacity as Bank of Italy governor, Draghi was also a member of the governing and general councils of the <a href="/wiki/European_Central_Bank" title="European Central Bank">European Central Bank</a> and a member of the board of directors of the <a href="/wiki/Bank_for_International_Settlements" title="Bank for International Settlements">Bank for International Settlements</a>. He also represented Italy on the board of governors at both the <a href="/wiki/International_Bank_for_Reconstruction_and_Development" title="International Bank for Reconstruction and Development">International Bank for Reconstruction and Development</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Asian_Development_Bank" title="Asian Development Bank">Asian Development Bank</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-SymposiumCity2009_47-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SymposiumCity2009-47"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 5 August 2011, he made a contribution to domestic political debate when, together with the <a href="/wiki/European_Central_Bank" title="European Central Bank">ECB President</a> <a href="/wiki/Jean_Claude_Trichet" class="mw-redirect" title="Jean Claude Trichet">Jean Claude Trichet</a>, he published a <a href="/wiki/Trichet-Draghi_letter" title="Trichet-Draghi letter">notable letter</a> to the <a href="/wiki/Berlusconi_IV_Cabinet" class="mw-redirect" title="Berlusconi IV Cabinet">Italian Government</a> of <a href="/wiki/Silvio_Berlusconi" title="Silvio Berlusconi">Silvio Berlusconi</a> to recommend a series of economic measures that should urgently be implemented in Italy.<sup id="cite_ref-Pisani-Ferry2014_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Pisani-Ferry2014-48"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="President_of_the_European_Central_Bank_(2011–2019)"><span id="President_of_the_European_Central_Bank_.282011.E2.80.932019.29"></span>President of the European Central Bank (2011–2019)</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: President of the European Central Bank (2011–2019)"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Strauss-Kahn,_Trichet,_Draghi_(IMF_2009).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Strauss-Kahn%2C_Trichet%2C_Draghi_%28IMF_2009%29.jpg/250px-Strauss-Kahn%2C_Trichet%2C_Draghi_%28IMF_2009%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Strauss-Kahn%2C_Trichet%2C_Draghi_%28IMF_2009%29.jpg/500px-Strauss-Kahn%2C_Trichet%2C_Draghi_%28IMF_2009%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2000"></a><figcaption>Draghi (right) with <a href="/wiki/Dominique_Strauss-Kahn" title="Dominique Strauss-Kahn">Dominique Strauss-Kahn</a> and <a href="/wiki/Jean-Claude_Trichet" title="Jean-Claude Trichet">Jean-Claude Trichet</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Draghi had for years been mentioned as a possible successor to <a href="/wiki/Jean-Claude_Trichet" title="Jean-Claude Trichet">Jean-Claude Trichet</a>, whose term as president of the <a href="/wiki/European_Central_Bank" title="European Central Bank">European Central Bank</a> was due to end in October 2011.<sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 13 February 2011, Wolfgang Münchau, associate editor of the <i><a href="/wiki/Financial_Times" title="Financial Times">Financial Times</a></i>, endorsed Draghi as the best candidate for the position.<sup id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> A few days later, <i><a href="/wiki/The_Economist" title="The Economist">The Economist</a></i> wrote that "the next president of the world's second-most-important central bank should be Mario Draghi".<sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi subsequently won the support of Italian prime minister <a href="/wiki/Silvio_Berlusconi" title="Silvio Berlusconi">Silvio Berlusconi</a> for the position, who expressed a desire to see an Italian take the pre-eminent economic policymaking role within the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-52"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 17 May 2011, the <a href="/wiki/Council_of_the_European_Union" title="Council of the European Union">Council of the European Union</a> recommended the nomination of Draghi as President of the ECB.<sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi's nomination was later approved by the <a href="/wiki/European_Parliament" title="European Parliament">European Parliament</a> and the ECB itself, and on 24 June 2011 his appointment was signed-off by EU leaders.<sup id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-WSJ01_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-WSJ01-55"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During the nomination process, some concerns were raised about Draghi's past employment at <a href="/wiki/Goldman_Sachs" title="Goldman Sachs">Goldman Sachs</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-accounting-tricks_42-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-accounting-tricks-42"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> As a member of the <a href="/wiki/Group_of_Thirty" title="Group of Thirty">Group of Thirty</a>, founded by the <a href="/wiki/Rockefeller_Foundation" title="Rockefeller Foundation">Rockefeller Foundation</a>, he was accused in <i><a href="/wiki/Der_Spiegel" title="Der Spiegel">Der Spiegel</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Tagesschau.de" class="mw-redirect" title="Tagesschau.de">Tagesschau.de</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/Die_Welt" title="Die Welt">Die Welt</a></i> of having a conflict of interest as president of the ECB.<sup id="cite_ref-bisbm_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bisbm-57"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi moved to <a href="/wiki/Frankfurt" title="Frankfurt">Frankfurt</a> and formally took up the role of ECB President on 1 November 2011, the day after Trichet's term expired.<sup id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-59"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In December 2011, Draghi brokered a €489 billion three-year loan program from the ECB to EU banks. Draghi's ECB also promptly repealed the final two interest rate hikes of Trichet's term, stating this would ease the <a href="/wiki/Euro_area_crisis" title="Euro area crisis">Euro area crisis</a>. In February 2012, Nobel Prize laureate in economics, <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Stiglitz" title="Joseph Stiglitz">Joseph Stiglitz</a> argued that on the issue of the impending <a href="/wiki/Greek_government-debt_crisis" title="Greek government-debt crisis">Greek government-debt crisis</a>, the ECB's insistence that it should be "voluntary", as opposed to a default agreed by Greek authorities, would be "a gift" to the financial institutions that sold credit default insurance on that debt, a position Stiglitz argued was a <a href="/wiki/Moral_hazard" title="Moral hazard">moral hazard</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In March 2012, a second, larger round of ECB loans to EU banks was initiated, this time called the <a href="/wiki/LTRO" class="mw-redirect" title="LTRO">Long-Term Refinancing Operation</a> (LTRO). One commentator, <a href="/wiki/Matthew_Lynn" title="Matthew Lynn">Matthew Lynn</a>, saw the ECB's injection of funds, along with <a href="/wiki/Quantitative_easing" title="Quantitative easing">quantitative easing</a> from the US <a href="/wiki/Federal_Reserve" title="Federal Reserve">Federal Reserve</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Bank_of_England" title="Bank of England">Bank of England</a>, as feeding increases in <a href="/wiki/Oil_prices" class="mw-redirect" title="Oil prices">oil prices</a> in <a href="/wiki/World_oil_market_chronology_from_2003#2011" title="World oil market chronology from 2003">2011</a> and <a href="/wiki/World_oil_market_chronology_from_2003#2012" title="World oil market chronology from 2003">2012</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mario_Draghi_World_Economic_Forum_2013.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Mario_Draghi_World_Economic_Forum_2013.jpg/250px-Mario_Draghi_World_Economic_Forum_2013.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="158" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Mario_Draghi_World_Economic_Forum_2013.jpg/500px-Mario_Draghi_World_Economic_Forum_2013.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4604" data-file-height="2912"></a><figcaption>Draghi in <a href="/wiki/Davos" title="Davos">Davos</a> in 2013</figcaption></figure>
<p>In July 2012, in the midst of renewed fears about sovereigns in the eurozone, Draghi stated in a panel discussion that, under his leadership, the ECB "is ready to do <i>whatever it takes</i> to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough."<sup id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This statement was heavily reported throughout the EU and the world's financial markets, and initially led to a steady decline in bond yields (borrowing costs) for eurozone countries, in particular Spain, Italy and France. In light of what had been slow political progress on solving the eurozone crisis, Draghi's statement has come to be seen subsequently as the major turning point in the fortunes of the eurozone, with numerous policymakers and commentators describing it as having been essential to the continuation of the euro currency.<sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Draghi has since come to be prominently associated with the phrase "whatever it takes". Beginning in 2013, Draghi was criticised in the context of the scandals rising around the bank <a href="/wiki/Banca_Monte_dei_Paschi_di_Siena" title="Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena">Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> which according to at least one German publication was making very risky deals.<sup id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Twenty_years_of_the_euro_three_in_four_Europeans_are_in_favour_of_the_single_currency_(39786518243).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Twenty_years_of_the_euro_three_in_four_Europeans_are_in_favour_of_the_single_currency_%2839786518243%29.jpg/250px-Twenty_years_of_the_euro_three_in_four_Europeans_are_in_favour_of_the_single_currency_%2839786518243%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Twenty_years_of_the_euro_three_in_four_Europeans_are_in_favour_of_the_single_currency_%2839786518243%29.jpg/500px-Twenty_years_of_the_euro_three_in_four_Europeans_are_in_favour_of_the_single_currency_%2839786518243%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1365"></a><figcaption>Draghi during a plenary session of the <a href="/wiki/European_Parliament" title="European Parliament">European Parliament</a> in 2019</figcaption></figure>
<p>In April 2013, Draghi said in response to a question regarding membership of the eurozone, "These questions are formulated by people who vastly underestimate what the euro means for the Europeans, for the euro area. They vastly underestimate the political capital that has been invested in the euro."<sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 2015, in an appearance before the European Parliament, Draghi said that the future of the eurozone was at risk unless member countries gave up some independence and created more Pan-European government institutions. "We have not yet reached the stage of a genuine monetary union," Draghi said. Failure of eurozone countries to harmonise their economies and create stronger institutions would, he said, "put at risk the long-term success of the monetary union when faced with an important shock."<sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In 2015, Draghi said that his political ideas belong to <a href="/wiki/Liberal_socialism" title="Liberal socialism">liberal socialism</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 31 October 2019, his mandate as ECB President expired and <a href="/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund" title="International Monetary Fund">International Monetary Fund Managing Director</a> <a href="/wiki/Christine_Lagarde" title="Christine Lagarde">Christine Lagarde</a> was appointed as his successor.<sup id="cite_ref-appointment-ECB_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-appointment-ECB-70"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Prime_Minister_of_Italy_(2021–2022)"><span id="Prime_Minister_of_Italy_.282021.E2.80.932022.29"></span>Prime Minister of Italy (2021–2022)</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Prime Minister of Italy (2021–2022)"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Government_formation">Government formation</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Government formation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1353705441">.mw-parser-output .hatnote{font-style:italic}.mw-parser-output div.hatnote{padding-left:1.6em;margin-bottom:0.5em}.mw-parser-output .hatnote i{font-style:normal}.mw-parser-output .hatnote+span.mw-empty-elt+.hatnote,.mw-parser-output .hatnote+link+.hatnote{margin-top:-0.5em}@media print{body.ns-0 .mw-parser-output .hatnote{display:none!important}}</style><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/2021_Italian_government_crisis" title="2021 Italian government crisis">2021 Italian government crisis</a> and <a href="/wiki/Draghi_Cabinet" class="mw-redirect" title="Draghi Cabinet">Draghi Cabinet</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mattarella_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Mattarella_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg/250px-Mattarella_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="168" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Mattarella_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg/500px-Mattarella_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2378" data-file-height="1598"></a><figcaption>Draghi with President <a href="/wiki/Sergio_Mattarella" title="Sergio Mattarella">Sergio Mattarella</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Quirinal_Palace" title="Quirinal Palace">Quirinal Palace</a> on 3 February 2021</figcaption></figure>
<p>Between December 2020 and January 2021, tensions arose within Italy's ruling coalition, with Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Giuseppe_Conte" title="Giuseppe Conte">Giuseppe Conte</a> and former prime minister <a href="/wiki/Matteo_Renzi" title="Matteo Renzi">Matteo Renzi</a> taking contrary positions on the management of the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Italy" title="COVID-19 pandemic in Italy">COVID-19 pandemic in Italy</a> as well as its deep economic consequences.<sup id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-71"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 13 January, Renzi announced the resignation of the two Cabinet Ministers from his party, <a href="/wiki/Italia_Viva" title="Italia Viva">Italia Viva</a>, triggering the collapse of the <a href="/wiki/Conte_II_Cabinet" class="mw-redirect" title="Conte II Cabinet">second Conte Government</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-72"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 26 January, after days of inconclusive negotiations with political parties, Conte tendered his resignation as prime minister to President Mattarella.<sup id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-73"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 2 February 2021, following failed consultations between parties to nominate a replacement, President Mattarella announced he would summon Draghi to the <a href="/wiki/Quirinal_Palace" title="Quirinal Palace">Quirinal Palace</a>, with the intention of giving him the task of forming a <a href="/wiki/Technocratic" class="mw-redirect" title="Technocratic">technocratic</a> government.<sup id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-75"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-76"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The following day, Draghi accepted the task of forming a new government and began consultations with party leaders.<sup id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-77"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi quickly secured the support of the centre-left <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Party_(Italy)" title="Democratic Party (Italy)">Democratic Party</a> (PD), the centrist <a href="/wiki/Italia_Viva" title="Italia Viva">Italia Viva</a> (IV), the left-wing <a href="/wiki/Free_and_Equal_(Italy)" title="Free and Equal (Italy)">Free and Equal</a> (LeU), and other small liberal and centrist parties.<sup id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-78"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> After an initial delay, <a href="/wiki/Matteo_Salvini" title="Matteo Salvini">Matteo Salvini</a>, leader of the right-wing <a href="/wiki/Lega_Nord" title="Lega Nord">League</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Silvio_Berlusconi" title="Silvio Berlusconi">Silvio Berlusconi</a>, leader of the centre-right <span title="Italian-language text"><span lang="it" style="font-style: normal;"><a href="/wiki/Forza_Italia_(2013)" title="Forza Italia (2013)">Forza Italia</a></span></span>, jointly announced they too would support Draghi.<sup id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-79"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Finally, on 11 February, the membership of the <a href="/wiki/Five_Star_Movement" title="Five Star Movement">Five Star Movement</a> (M5S) approved the party's support for Draghi, with 59.3% of party members voting in favour of joining the new government.<sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Governo_Draghi.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Governo_Draghi.jpg/250px-Governo_Draghi.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="168" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Governo_Draghi.jpg/500px-Governo_Draghi.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2378" data-file-height="1598"></a><figcaption>Draghi and his Cabinet at the Quirinal Palace after the oath of office</figcaption></figure>
<p>On 12 February, Draghi unveiled the members of <a href="/wiki/Draghi_Cabinet" class="mw-redirect" title="Draghi Cabinet">his Cabinet</a>, which included representatives from all of the above political parties, including 9 ministers from the outgoing cabinet, as well as independent technocrats.<sup id="cite_ref-NYT_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NYT-81"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The following day, Draghi was sworn in as prime minister. Draghi's cabinet was described as a <a href="/wiki/National_unity_government" title="National unity government">national unity government</a> in the wake of its announcement.<sup id="cite_ref-FT_82-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FT-82"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-83"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>83<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 17 February, Draghi won a confidence vote in the <a href="/wiki/Italian_Senate" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian Senate">Senate</a>, with 262 votes in favour, 40 against and 2 abstentions.<sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>85<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On the following day, he won a further confidence vote in the <a href="/wiki/Chamber_of_Deputies_(Italy)" title="Chamber of Deputies (Italy)">Chamber of Deputies</a> with 535 votes in favour, 56 against and 5 abstentions; this margin represented one of the largest ever majorities in the history of the Italian Republic.<sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>86<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During his first speech as prime minister to both houses of the <a href="/wiki/Italian_Parliament" title="Italian Parliament">Italian Parliament</a>, Draghi stated that the Italy that emerged after the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Italy" title="COVID-19 pandemic in Italy">COVID-19 pandemic</a> would have to undergo a period of reconstruction similar to <a href="/wiki/Post-World_War_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Post-World War II">post-World War II</a> Italy, and that it would be his government's responsibility to begin this process.<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> He also stressed that his government would adopt a strongly pro-European position, and emphasised the importance of Italy remaining within the <a href="/wiki/Eurosystem" title="Eurosystem">Eurosystem</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-88" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-88"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>88<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-90"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 13 May, it was announced that Draghi would forgo his annual salary of €115,000 for being prime minister.<sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>92<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="COVID-19_pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: COVID-19 pandemic"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Italy" title="COVID-19 pandemic in Italy">COVID-19 pandemic in Italy</a> and <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_vaccination_in_Italy" title="COVID-19 vaccination in Italy">COVID-19 vaccination in Italy</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mario_Draghi_-_May_2021.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Mario_Draghi_-_May_2021.jpg/250px-Mario_Draghi_-_May_2021.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="173" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Mario_Draghi_-_May_2021.jpg/500px-Mario_Draghi_-_May_2021.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3072" data-file-height="2126"></a><figcaption>Mario Draghi in May 2021</figcaption></figure>
<p>Addressing the nation shortly after becoming prime minister, Draghi stated that it would be his government's priority to plan a route out of the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic" title="COVID-19 pandemic">COVID-19 pandemic</a>, and pledged to reorganise the country's pandemic response units; on 27 February, Draghi replaced the Head of the <a href="/wiki/Protezione_Civile" title="Protezione Civile">Civil Protection</a>, <a href="/wiki/Angelo_Borrelli" title="Angelo Borrelli">Angelo Borrelli</a>, with <a href="/wiki/Fabrizio_Curcio" title="Fabrizio Curcio">Fabrizio Curcio</a>, and on 1 March, he replaced the Extraordinary Commissioner for the COVID-19 Emergency, <a href="/wiki/Domenico_Arcuri" title="Domenico Arcuri">Domenico Arcuri</a>, with the <a href="/wiki/Italian_Army" title="Italian Army">Army</a> General <a href="/wiki/Francesco_Paolo_Figliuolo" title="Francesco Paolo Figliuolo">Francesco Paolo Figliuolo</a>, who received the additional mandate of reorganising and implementing the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_vaccination_in_Italy" title="COVID-19 vaccination in Italy">vaccination campaign</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Borrelli and Arcuri had both been considered close to former prime minister Giuseppe Conte.<sup id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-94"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Following discussions with European Commission President <a href="/wiki/Ursula_von_der_Leyen" title="Ursula von der Leyen">Ursula von der Leyen</a>, Draghi announced that he had agreed to ensure vaccines produced in Italy were prioritised for distribution to the population of the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-96"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On the following day, Draghi made international headlines by authorising the blocking of a shipment of 250,000 <a href="/wiki/Oxford%E2%80%93AstraZeneca_COVID-19_vaccine" title="Oxford–AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine">Oxford–AstraZeneca vaccines</a> that were originally intended to travel to Australia.<sup id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>97<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> This led to harsh criticism by Australian prime minister <a href="/wiki/Scott_Morrison" title="Scott Morrison">Scott Morrison</a> and British prime minister <a href="/wiki/Boris_Johnson" title="Boris Johnson">Boris Johnson</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-98"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>98<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>99<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Conversely, Draghi's decision was praised by other European leaders, such as French President <a href="/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron" title="Emmanuel Macron">Emmanuel Macron</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> In mid-March, the Italian Government announced it would pause the rollout of the Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine, after reports that some Italians treated with it had developed blood clots, although no death cases have been reported directly due to the vaccine.<sup id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>101<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> 
On 16 March 2021, Draghi had a phone call with the French President Macron concerning the suspension of the AstraZeneca vaccine and of the eventual decisions of the <a href="/wiki/European_Medicines_Agency" title="European Medicines Agency">European Medicines Agency</a> that will take a definitive decision on 18 March 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>102<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 15 March 2021, Draghi placed the majority of Italy under so-called 'full lockdown' conditions, with non-essential businesses closing and travel restricted, in response to an increase in the transmission of COVID-19, although unlike the 2020 lockdown, factories and some other workplaces were allowed to remain open. Announcing the lockdown, Draghi vowed that Italy would see its vaccination programme triple in April, reaching 500,000 people per day by that time.<sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>103<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Around this time, Draghi's approval rating as prime minister reached a new high of 63% in opinion polls.<sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 16 April, during a press conference with his health minister <a href="/wiki/Roberto_Speranza" title="Roberto Speranza">Roberto Speranza</a>, Draghi announced that restrictions will be eased from 26 April, allowing the reopening of bars and restaurants, stating that "it is possible to look to the future with prudent optimism and confidence".<sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>From the summer of 2021 to 2022, Italy had greatly suffered from the highly transmissible <a href="/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Delta_variant" title="SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant">Delta</a> <a href="/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Omicron_variant" title="SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant">cron</a> hybrid variant that is combined with Delta and Omicron variant, also known as the recombination event, for example: In June 2021, COVID-19 Delta variant has caused a surge in COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in Italy, especially among all of those who are unvaccinated or fully vaccinated.<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>106<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>108<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> To contain the spread of new variants, in August of the same year, Italian government extended the requirement of the <a href="/wiki/Immunity_passport#EU_Digital_COVID_Certificate" title="Immunity passport">EU Digital COVID Certificate</a>, also known as "Green Pass", to the participation in sports events and music festivals, but also to the access to indoor places like bars, restaurants, and gyms, as well as to long-distance public transportation.<sup id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-109"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 15 October of the same year, Italy became the first country in the world to established both mandatory <a href="/wiki/Vaccine_passports_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic" title="Vaccine passports during the COVID-19 pandemic">COVID-19 vaccination certificate</a> and/or <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_testing" title="COVID-19 testing">negative test</a>, for the entire work force, public, and private.<sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>110<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 24 November of the same year, Draghi announced the introduction of COVID-19 vaccination certificate for all the recreational activities, like cinemas, bars, restaurants, and sport games; thus, eliminating the possibility of attending one of these activities with a negative test only.<sup id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-111"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 27 November 2021, <a href="/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Omicron_variant" title="SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant">COVID-19 Omicron variant</a> has arrived in Italy. However, as the country became widespread, Italy has now causing a massive increase in cases, hospitalizations, and deaths. On 5 January 2022, amid the spread of COVID-19 Deltacron hybrid variant, Italian government introduced <a href="/wiki/Compulsory_vaccination" class="mw-redirect" title="Compulsory vaccination">compulsory vaccination</a> for all Italian citizens above the age of 50.<sup id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-112"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>112<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Domestic_reforms">Domestic reforms</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Domestic reforms"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mattarella_Draghi_2022.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Mattarella_Draghi_2022.jpg/250px-Mattarella_Draghi_2022.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Mattarella_Draghi_2022.jpg/500px-Mattarella_Draghi_2022.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3543" data-file-height="2362"></a><figcaption>Mario Draghi and Sergio Mattarella on 3 February 2022</figcaption></figure>
<p>In July and August, Draghi led the process to overhaul Italy's criminal and civil justice system, with an aim of reducing the time taken to resolve cases. Among other things, the reform package abolished one of the two levels of appeal applied to most cases in the Italian judiciary. The reforms had long been argued for by several political parties, on the basis that the slow legal system disincentivised external investment into Italy.<sup id="cite_ref-euronews.com_114-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-euronews.com-114"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 3 August 2021, the package of reforms passed the Italian Parliament after Draghi announced that he would consider the vote a question of confidence in his government.<sup id="cite_ref-euronews.com_114-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-euronews.com-114"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi also announced that the passage of judicial overhaul would be linked to the allocation of €200bn in post-pandemic stimulus funds from the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a>. The judicial overhaul represented the first successful reform package of the Italian justice system in several decades.<sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>115<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In October 2021, the Draghi Government passed its <a href="/wiki/Government_budget" title="Government budget">budget</a> for 2022. The budget modified the pension reform approved by the Conte Government, known as <i>Quota 100</i>, which enabled retirement at age 62 with 38 years of contributions, introducing instead the so-called <i>Quota 102</i> (which allows retirement at age 64 with 38 years of contributions).<sup id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-116"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>116<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Italian trade unions opposed the reform and organised a general strike in protest in late November and early December 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The Draghi government's budget also modified the <a href="/wiki/Citizens%27_income_(Italy)" title="Citizens' income (Italy)">citizens' income</a>, a universal basic income introduced by Conte. The new income introduces a gradual decline in the allowance after six months and its revocation after two rejected job offers.<sup id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-118"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>118<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 30 December 2021, Draghi oversaw passage of an additional budget proposal, including an overhaul of the Italian taxation system, the introduction of a new series of tax credits and wide-ranging company tax cuts, subsidies for firms that hire young people and new mothers, subsidised mortgages for people buying their first property, and a fund set aside in order to mitigate rising energy prices.<sup id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-119"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> At the end of 2021, the <i><a href="/wiki/Economist_Magazine" class="mw-redirect" title="Economist Magazine">Economist</a></i> magazine named Italy as its 'Country of the Year', awarded each year to the country judged to have made the most improvement over the course of one year. The magazine singled out Draghi's leadership as central to the decision.<sup id="cite_ref-wantedinrome.com_21-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wantedinrome.com-21"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In the <a href="/wiki/2022_Italian_presidential_election" title="2022 Italian presidential election">2022 presidential election</a>, Draghi was widely seen as a probable successor of incumbent president <a href="/wiki/Sergio_Mattarella" title="Sergio Mattarella">Sergio Mattarella</a>. However, on 29 January 2022, Draghi publicly supported the re-election of Mattarella as president, ending media speculation that he himself could succeed Mattarella, and pledged to oversee an overhaul of Italian competition law and public procurement policy in the following six months, with a view to increase the performance of the economy.<sup id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-120"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 18 February 2022, amid the <a href="/wiki/2021%E2%80%932022_global_energy_crisis" class="mw-redirect" title="2021–2022 global energy crisis">global energy crisis</a>, the Draghi Government approved a package of €8bn euro to support the economy, heavily affected by the rise of energy costs.<sup id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-121"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>121<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Foreign_policies">Foreign policies</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Mario_Draghi&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Foreign policies"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<figure class="mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Draghi_Biden_2021_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Draghi_Biden_2021_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Draghi_Biden_2021_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="331" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Draghi_Biden_2021_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Draghi_Biden_2021_%28cropped%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1246" data-file-height="1649"></a><figcaption>Mario Draghi with the U.S. President <a href="/wiki/Joe_Biden" title="Joe Biden">Joe Biden</a> in October 2021 in Rome</figcaption></figure>
<p>Since the beginning of his premiership, Draghi implemented an active foreign policy focused on the <a href="/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea" title="Mediterranean Sea">Mediterranean Sea</a>, North Africa and the Middle East in order to increase Italy's influence over the area.<sup id="cite_ref-122" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-122"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>122<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-123"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>123<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 6 April 2021, Draghi visited <a href="/wiki/Libya" title="Libya">Libya</a>, in his <a href="/wiki/List_of_international_prime_ministerial_trips_made_by_Mario_Draghi" title="List of international prime ministerial trips made by Mario Draghi">first international trip</a>, during which he met Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Abdul_Hamid_Dbeibeh" title="Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh">Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh</a>, saying he wanted to strengthen ties with the African country, a former colony of Italy.<sup id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-124"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>124<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The trip was described as an attempt to reduce the Turkish and Egyptian influences over Libya, following the aftermath of the <a href="/wiki/Libyan_Civil_War_(2014%E2%80%93present)" class="mw-redirect" title="Libyan Civil War (2014–present)">civil war</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-125" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-125"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>125<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Days later, Draghi publicly labelled Turkish President <a href="/wiki/Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan" title="Recep Tayyip Erdoğan">Recep Tayyip Erdoğan</a> as a "dictator", harshly criticising him for his behaviour after a meeting with European leaders <a href="/wiki/Ursula_von_der_Leyen" title="Ursula von der Leyen">Ursula von der Leyen</a> and <a href="/wiki/Charles_Michel" title="Charles Michel">Charles Michel</a>, during which, according to Draghi, he "<a href="/wiki/Sofagate" title="Sofagate">humiliated President von der Leyen</a>".<sup id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-126"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>126<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-127"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>127<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The statement caused immediate reactions from the Turkish government. Turkey's foreign minister <a href="/wiki/Mevl%C3%BCt_%C3%87avu%C5%9Fo%C4%9Flu" title="Mevlüt Çavuşoğlu">Mevlüt Çavuşoğlu</a> summoned Italian ambassador and described Draghi's words as an "unacceptable populist rhetoric", while many other prominent members of Erdoğan's cabinet strongly attacked Draghi.<sup id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-128"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>128<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-129"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>129<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> However, Draghi was backed by several European leaders, including the head of the <a href="/wiki/European_People%27s_Party" title="European People's Party">European People's Party</a>, <a href="/wiki/Manfred_Weber" title="Manfred Weber">Manfred Weber</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-130"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>130<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> On 14 April, Erdoğan accused Draghi of being an "appointed and unelected Prime Minister", describing his statement as "rude and impertinent".<sup id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-131"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>131<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-132"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>132<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Macron_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Macron_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg/250px-Macron_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="168" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Macron_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg/500px-Macron_Draghi_Quirinale_2021.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2378" data-file-height="1598"></a><figcaption>Draghi and the <a href="/wiki/French_President" class="mw-redirect" title="French President">French President</a> <a href="/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron" title="Emmanuel Macron">Emmanuel Macron</a>, in 2021, following the signing of the <a href="/wiki/Quirinal_Treaty" title="Quirinal Treaty">Quirinal Treaty</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>In June 2021, Draghi attended his first <a href="/wiki/G7" title="G7">G7</a> summit in <a href="/wiki/Cornwall" title="Cornwall">Cornwall</a> in the United Kingdom. During the meeting, Draghi led discussions on strategy for avoiding adverse market reactions to stimulus spending.<sup id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-133"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>133<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> During the summit, Draghi held a bilateral meeting with U.S. President <a href="/wiki/Joe_Biden" title="Joe Biden">Joe Biden</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-134"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>134<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Draghi praised Biden, saying he had improved relations between the European Union and the United States.<sup id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-135"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>135<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In August 2021, following the withdrawal of NATO troops from <a href="/wiki/Afghanistan" title="Afghanistan">Afghanistan</a> amid the <a href="/wiki/2021_Taliban_offensive" title="2021 Taliban offensive">Taliban offensive</a>, the Italian government took part in the <a href="/wiki/2021_evacuation_from_Afghanistan" class="mw-redirect" title="2021 evacuation from Afghanistan">evacuation from Kabul</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-136" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-136"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>136<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> Within the Operation "Aquila Omnia",<sup id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-137"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> nearly 5,000 Afghans were evacuated by the <a href="/wiki/Italian_Armed_Forces" title="Italian Armed Forces">Italian Armed Forces</a> and brought to Italy.<sup id="cite_ref-138" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-138"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>138<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 30 and 31 October 2021, Rome hosted the annual <a href="/wiki/2021_G20_Rome_summit" title="2021 G20 Rome summit">G20 summit</a>. Draghi and the other leaders mainly discussed climate change, COVID-19 pandemic and post-pandemic global recovery in health, economic and political terms. The only leaders who did not attend the G20 were the <a href="/wiki/Paramount_leader" title="Paramount leader">Chinese leader</a> <a href="/wiki/Xi_Jinping" title="Xi Jinping">Xi Jinping</a> and the Russian President <a href="/wiki/Vladimir_Putin" title="Vladimir Putin">Vladimir Putin</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-139" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-139"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>139<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p><p>On 26 November 2021, Draghi signed the "<a href="/wiki/Quirinal_Treaty" title="Quirinal Treaty">Quirinal Treaty</a>", with the French president <a href="/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron" title="Emmanuel Macron">Emmanuel Macron</a>, at the <a href="/wiki/Quirinal_Palace" title="Quirinal Palace">Quirinal Palace</a>, in Rome.<sup id="cite_ref-140" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-140"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>140<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup> The treaty is aimed to promote the convergence and coordination of French and Italian positions in matters of European and foreign policies, security and defence, migration policy, economy, education, research, culture and cross-border cooperation.<sup id="cite_ref-141" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-141"><span class="cite-bracket">[</span>141<span class="cite-bracket">]</span></a></sup>
</p>
